items.title: [@enspirit/elo] Elo JavaScript emitter has sandbox escape to arbitrary Node.js / browser code execution via unfiltered `.constructor` member access
items.summary: SummaryAn unauthenticated attacker who controls a string passed to any Elo JavaScript-emission path — defaultFormats.elo.parse(), the bin/elo CLI, or the live browser playground at elo-lang.org/try — can execute arbitrary code in the host JavaScript runtime. A payload built from the .constructor.constructor chain compiles, without modification, to a live Function invocation in the emitted JavaScript, escaping any sandbox assumption around "Elo is a safe data/DSL language."Vulnerable sink and root causeThree interacting sites in src/ produce the bug at commit 749af7b:src/transform.ts:144–158 — the member_access handler allows access on types any, object, or array without filtering the property name. This is the only place an integrator could have plugged a denylist.src/compilers/javascript.ts:210 — the JS emitter writes ${objectExpr}.${ir.property} verbatim into the output, so any property name that survives the transform step flows unescaped into emitted JavaScript.src/parser.ts:163–170, 748–750 — the parser accepts constructor (and other JS meta-property names) as an ordinary identifier, so .constructor clears type-checking without triggering any warning.Combined, the Elo expression ({}).constructor.constructor('…')() compiles to a live Function('…')() call in the emitted JS, executing in the realm of whichever sink runs the compiled code.Attack surfacesAll three surfaces share the same root cause (no denylist in transform.ts) and are addressed by the same one-file patch:#Entry pointThreat model1Browser playground — https://elo-lang.org/try/?code=…&run=10-click XSS / account takeover against elo-lang.org. ?run=1 triggers setTimeout(() => this.run(), 100) in playground_controller.ts:531; the server issues a 301 that preserves ?code=. Any shared URL that contains a payload compromises the visitor's session on elo-lang.org.2bin/elo CLIRCE on CI / DevOps hosts. Both node bin/elo payload.elo and node bin/elo -e "_" -d @payload.elo -f elo fire. The -f elo path is especially severe: the flag exists to pass user-supplied files as data into an Elo pipeline. No integrator expects a data-format flag to shell out to /usr/bin/id.3Library API — defaultFormats.elo.parse()Node.js RCE for any downstream integrator using Elo as a rule engine, configuration DSL, or form builder DSL (the primary documented use cases).Proof of ConceptCommon payload (works on all three entry points):({}).constructor.constructor('return this.constructor.constructor(\'return process\')().mainModule.require(\'child_process\').execSync(\'id\').toString()')()Library API — poc-minimal.js:// npm install eloconst { defaultFormats } = require('elo');const payload = "({}).constructor.constructor('return this.constructor.constructor(\\'return process\\')().mainModule.require(\\'child_process\\').execSync(\\'id\\').toString()')()";console.log(defaultFormats.elo.parse(payload));// → uid=1000(ultrasupara) gid=1000(ultrasupara) groups=…CLI — poc-cli.sh:node bin/elo payload.elo# uid=1000(ultrasupara)…node bin/elo -e "_" -d @payload.elo -f elo# uid=1000(ultrasupara)…Browser playground — 0-click XSS URL:https://elo-lang.org/try/?code=%28%7B%7D%29.constructor.constructor%28%27alert%28document.domain%29%27%29%28%29&run=1Opening this URL causes alert(document.domain) to fire automatically after ~100 ms with no user interaction beyond navigating to the link. The 301 redirect preserves the ?code= parameter intact. End-to-end execution on the live production site was captured in a screen recording attached to the original report.Independence from GHSA #3 (AST-API injection)This finding is independent of the Medium-severity AST-API report (GHSA #3). That fix's identifier regex ^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$ happens to accept constructor, and its threat model requires an attacker-controlled AST object rather than a plain string. The current finding requires only a plain Elo string, which is a strictly weaker attacker model.Referenceshttps://github.com/enspirit/elo/security/advisories/GHSA-33r5-xmm8-v6x5https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-33r5-xmm8-v6x5

items.title: [@enspirit/elo] Elo Ruby backend has Remote Code Execution via unescaped `#{...}` interpolation in emitted string literals and subtype-constraint labels
items.summary: SummaryElo's Ruby backend emits attacker-controlled text into Ruby double-quoted strings without escaping the # character. Because # begins Ruby's interpolation sequences — #{expr}, #@ivar, #@@cvar, #$gvar — and any expression wrapped in #{...} may use backticks for shell execution, an Elo program that contains a crafted string literal or a labelled subtype constraint compiles to Ruby that evaluates attacker-chosen Ruby, and through backticks runs attacker-chosen shell commands, at runtime.The same Elo source compiled to JavaScript, Python, or SQL is benign, so the bug also breaks the cross-target portability guarantee the rest of the compiler honours.Vulnerable sinksTwo sinks exist in src/compilers/ruby.ts at commit 749af7b:String-literal emitter — lines 180–184.The emitter escapes backslash, double quote, and control characters, but not #. Any #{...} sequence in an Elo string literal flows straight into the emitted Ruby source.Labelled subtype-constraint branch — lines 405–412.The error message passed to p_fail(p, "...") is wrapped in a Ruby double-quoted string with no escape pass at all. Because the parser at src/parser.ts:1339–1348 accepts single-quoted Elo strings as constraint labels, a label such as '#{ `id` }' flows unchanged into the emitted Ruby.Attack surfacesAll three surfaces share the same root cause (the missing # escape in the Ruby double-quoted-string emission path) and are addressed by the same patch:#Entry pointThreat model1/try playground on elo-lang.org (Ruby target)0-click server-side RCE against elo-lang.org infrastructure from a shared PoC URL2bin/eloc -t ruby -x on a CI or DevOps hostRCE on any host that passes Elo strings through the CLI3Library API — defaultFormats.elo.parse() with a Ruby emission stepRuby RCE for any downstream integrator using Elo as a rule engine, configuration DSL, or form builder DSL (the primary documented use cases)Proof of ConceptString-literal sink:# poc.elo'RES=#{`id 2>&1`}'$ eloc -t ruby -x poc.elo# emitted Ruby contains:  "RES=#{`id 2>&1`}"# running it returns the output of id(1).Replacing `id 2>&1` with `touch /tmp/pwned` produces a trivially observable filesystem side effect.Subtype-constraint label sink:# poc-subtype.elolet X = Int(i | '#{`touch /tmp/pwned2`}': i > 0) in X(-1)The predicate fails for -1, causing p_fail(p, "#{...}") to interpolate and execute the backtick command at the Ruby layer.Both flows are automated in the reproduction script submitted with the original report and were verified against Ruby 3.x.Root causeThe Ruby-emitter's double-quoted-string escape routine omitted # from its character set, and one emission path (the subtype-constraint label branch) performed no escape pass at all.Referenceshttps://github.com/enspirit/elo/security/advisories/GHSA-7w38-ggh5-v542https://github.com/enspirit/elo/commit/51b869963fbe445c18328714a7ccfbd76b21ba38https://github.com/enspirit/elo/commit/d2a89a8db76a244eb740687524a7e8529b7554b5https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7w38-ggh5-v542

items.title: [@enspirit/elo] Elo backends have code injection via unvalidated emission of programmatic AST fields
items.summary: SummaryElo's programmatic AST API accepts arbitrary values in many node fields without runtime type or syntax validation. Each backend's emit stage interpolates those values straight into the generated source with no escape pass. An integrator that populates the AST from JSON-deserialised input, plugin output, or any other untyped source therefore exposes a code-injection primitive that flows through to the emitted JavaScript, Ruby, Python, or SQL.The same pattern was previously addressed in 0.9.7 (2026-01-27), which patched the date/datetime/duration literal emitters via JSON.stringify() after a report by naoyashiga. This advisory generalises that fix to the remaining AST surface — at least 23 emission sites across six node-field categories and four backends.Vulnerable sinksEach row is a category of sinks that share the same shape: TypeScript signature erased at runtime → AST-API consumer passes a crafted value → emit interpolates the value verbatim.#AST fieldAffected backendsResulting injection1int_literal / float_literal .valueJS, Ruby, Python, SQLArbitrary expression in the emitted numeric position (RCE on JS/Ruby/Python; SQL expression injection)2variable.nameJS, Ruby, Python, SQLIdentifier-position injection; on SQL, raw SQL injection because undefined identifiers are intentionally emitted as column references3member_access.propertyJS, Ruby, Python, SQLProperty access escaped into expression (RCE)4object_literal keyJS, Ruby, SQLComputed-key / extra-property injection (RCE on JS/Ruby; SQL injection)5datapath segmentJS, Ruby, Python, SQLRuby symbol-list injection allows backtick shell exec; SQL string-segment unquoted in single-quote context allows SQL injection6lambda.params[].nameJS, Ruby, PythonParameter-list structural injection (RCE)7SQL let binding nameSQLIdentifier injection in … AS <name> clauseProof of ConceptEnd-to-end execution was verified at commit 749af7b for representative cases per backend. Examples:Numeric literal injection (all four backends). Feeding the following AST through compileToJavaScript emits a live console.log on call:{ type: 'literal', value: "(console.log('PWN_INT_JS'),1)" }// emits: (function(_) { return (console.log('PWN_INT_JS'),1); })(null);The same AST against Ruby with "(system('touch /tmp/pwn_int_ruby'); 1)" creates the file; Python with "(print('PWN_INT_PY') or 1)" prints the sentinel; SQL emits the raw string into the numeric position.SQL variable.name injection:{ type: 'variable', name: "1; DROP TABLE users; --" }// emits: 1; DROP TABLE users; --Ruby datapath segment shell-exec:{ type: 'datapath', segments: ["a, system(`touch /tmp/pwn_dp_ruby`)"] }// emits: [:a, system(`touch /tmp/pwn_dp_ruby`)]All ten end-to-end cases are automated in the ast-exec.js / ast-exec2.js scripts attached to the original report; each console.log and sentinel file was observed.Independence from GHSA #2This finding is independent of GHSA #2 (the .constructor.constructor sandbox escape). That report covers payloads delivered as plain Elo strings through the parser; the present advisory covers payloads delivered as AST objects through the programmatic API. The two threat models do not overlap: GHSA #2's identifier regex ^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$ accepts constructor (and is the right behaviour for a parser), while the present advisory adds runtime validation at every backend emit site so that AST-API consumers cannot inject arbitrary text into emitted source.Referenceshttps://github.com/enspirit/elo/security/advisories/GHSA-x9rp-7wh3-2rj5https://github.com/enspirit/elo/commit/d2a89a8db76a244eb740687524a7e8529b7554b5https://github.com/enspirit/elo/commit/fb57dd37a2669d9c412454225c5b89a2adba5d93https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x9rp-7wh3-2rj5
